message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"c99bebe5f9901090a5304d61c2c9e83261fab3ac89bd0ea1b2e4f854c726e0c6","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-co-class-std:lineage:70","source_registry_sha256":"bdc8d5a61f622fc6c91da0be8478dfb02615c007374129c91888edf82eb1b746","units":[{"unit_id":"sec05-u01","module_id":"sec05-m01","objective_ids":["sec05-u01"],"title":{"text":"Backing up safely","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The space right behind a car is hidden from the driver seat and from the mirrors, so you must look before and while backing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"A slow, smooth reverse with your head turned gives you time to see and stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Mia is about to back out of her driveway, where neighborhood kids often play.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Small children cannot be seen from the driver seat, so she walks behind the car first, then reverses while looking over her shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"result":{"text":"Mia uses her camera along with her mirrors and a shoulder look, backs slowly, and keeps looking back until fully stopped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a rear-view camera means you no longer need to look over your shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"correction":{"text":"The camera is used together with mirrors and an over-the-shoulder look, never instead of them.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Look first, look back, go slow.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Your car has a rear-view camera. Can you rely on it alone when backing out?","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"No. Use it together with your mirrors and an over-the-shoulder look.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Mirrors miss the space right behind the car, and a camera never replaces looking back yourself.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Backing up safely","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Look before you get in.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Look back while reversing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Go slowly.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Backing up is one of the slowest things you do in a car, yet it causes many collisions, often with children or objects you never saw. This lesson walks through the handbook's backing routine from the moment you approach your vehicle. You will learn why to look behind the car before getting in, how to position your hands, arm and head while reversing, how a rear-view camera fits in, and how to control speed and steering when backing and turning. The routine is simple, but every step exists because the space behind a car is so hard to see.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Look before you get in","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Walk behind the vehicle first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Small children and objects hide there.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"They cannot be seen from the seat.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Before you get in to back up, look behind the vehicle. Small children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver seat, so the only way to know the space is clear is to check it on foot. A toddler sitting behind a bumper, a bicycle on the driveway or a pet lying in the shade can all be invisible once you are inside. This is especially important in driveways, parking lots and neighborhoods where children play. It takes only a few seconds to walk around the back of the car, and it can prevent a tragedy. Make it a habit.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Hands, arm and eyes","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Foot on the brake while shifting.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Left hand at the top of the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Right arm on the seat; look back.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To reverse, keep a foot on the brake while shifting into reverse. Grip the top of the steering wheel, the twelve o'clock spot, with your left hand. Rest your right arm on the back of the passenger seat and turn to look over your shoulder out the rear window. This position lets you twist far enough to see directly behind the car while still steering with one hand. Once you are moving, back up slowly and smoothly, steering a little toward where you want the rear of the car to go. Small steering movements are enough at low speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The camera is not enough","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mirrors miss the space right behind.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Camera plus mirrors plus a look.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Never instead of looking back.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Mirrors do not show the space right behind the car, and many drivers assume a rear-view camera solves the problem completely. The handbook says to use a camera, if you have one, together with mirrors and an over-the-shoulder look, never instead of them. A camera has its own blind areas, can be blurred by rain or dirt, and does not show cross traffic approaching from the sides. When a practice question suggests backing up while watching only the camera screen, that answer skips a required step. The look over your shoulder is still part of every reverse.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Camera only?","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"A car with a backup camera.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Is the camera enough?","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: your new car has a large rear-view camera screen, and a friend says you no longer need to turn around when backing out of a parking space. Is your friend right? Decide before reading on. No. The handbook says a rear-view camera is used together with mirrors and an over-the-shoulder look, never instead of them, because mirrors do not show the space right behind the car and cameras have limits too. When turning in reverse, also glance quickly to the front and sides, and keep looking back until you have fully stopped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Backing recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Check behind before getting in.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Hand at twelve, look back.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Slow, and keep looking.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. Before you get in to back up, look behind the vehicle, because small children and objects cannot be seen from the driver seat. To reverse, keep a foot on the brake while shifting, grip the top of the wheel with your left hand, rest your right arm on the passenger seat back and look over your shoulder. Use a rear-view camera together with mirrors and a shoulder look, never instead of them. Next, we look at who controls traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Who controls traffic","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"People directing traffic, such as officers and crossing guards, can respond to conditions that fixed signals cannot.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"A dark signal is handled as a four-way stop so that no driver assumes they have the right to go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A storm knocks out power and the traffic signal at a busy intersection goes dark as Raj approaches on the main road.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A dark or broken signal is handled as a four-way stop, and the busier road gets no special right to go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"result":{"text":"Raj comes to a full stop and takes his turn like every other driver at the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: assuming the busier road keeps going when a signal is dark.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05"]},"correction":{"text":"A dark signal is a four-way stop for everyone, not a green light for the busier road.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05","sec05-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Dark signal, everyone stops.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"The traffic signal ahead is completely dark. How should you handle the intersection?","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"answer":{"text":"As a four-way stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"A dark or broken signal is handled as a four-way stop, with no priority for the busier road.","fact_ids":["sec05-R05"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who is in charge","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signals, signs and markings.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"People who direct traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"When signals fail.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson sets up the rest of the chapter by answering a basic question: who or what controls traffic? You will meet the three kinds of fixed controls, which are signals, signs and pavement markings, and the people whose directions you must follow, such as police, highway workers and school crossing guards. Then we look at how traffic signals are usually arranged, and at an important situation that confuses many drivers: what to do when a signal goes dark or stops working. Knowing who is in charge at any moment keeps intersections predictable and safe.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Controls and people","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signals, signs and pavement markings.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Police, highway workers, crossing guards.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Follow their directions.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic is controlled by signals, signs and pavement markings. It is also controlled by people: police officers, highway workers and school crossing guards. You are required to follow their directions. When a person is directing traffic, their instructions take priority over the fixed signal. An officer might wave you through a red light to clear a crash, or a flagger might stop you on a green to protect workers. In those moments, follow the person. They can see conditions that the signal cannot respond to, and ignoring them is both dangerous and a violation.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"How signals are arranged","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red at the top.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Yellow in the middle.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Green at the bottom.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Signal lights are normally arranged with red at the top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom. This standard order helps everyone, including drivers who have trouble telling colors apart, because position alone tells you which light is lit. Some places use a single red, yellow or green light rather than a full stack. Whatever the arrangement, the meaning of each color stays the same. Learning the standard layout also helps at night or in glare, when the light itself may be hard to judge but its position in the housing is easier to read.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"When the signal is dark","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dark or broken: four-way stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"No green for the busier road.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. When a traffic signal is dark or not working properly, many drivers on the main road keep going as if they still had a green light. The handbook says to handle the intersection as a four-way stop. That means every driver, on every approach, comes to a full stop and takes turns. A dark or broken signal is not a green light for the busier road. Practice questions often describe a power outage and offer an answer that gives the main road priority. That answer is wrong. Stop, look, and take your turn like everyone else.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"A dark intersection","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"The signal is out.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"How do you proceed?","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: during a power outage you approach an intersection on a busy four-lane road, and the traffic signal is completely dark. Come to a full stop and take your turn with the other drivers. A dark or broken signal does not give the busier road the right to go. And if a police officer arrives to direct traffic, follow the officer's directions instead. Patience keeps everyone safe.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-R05","sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Traffic control recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Follow officers and crossing guards.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Red top, green bottom.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Dark signal: four-way stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. Signal lights are normally arranged with red at the top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom, though some places use a single light. Stay alert as you go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u03","module_id":"sec05-m03","objective_ids":["sec05-u03"],"title":{"text":"Steady red, yellow and green","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Turns on red are allowed only after a full stop and yield, so that pedestrians and cross traffic stay protected.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Green still requires yielding to people already in the intersection, because a green light is permission, not a guarantee.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lena is stopped at a steady red light on a one-way street, wanting to turn left onto another one-way street, with no sign against it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Left on red is legal only from one one-way street onto another, after stopping and yielding, with no sign prohibiting it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Lena yields to pedestrians and traffic, then turns left onto the one-way street.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a left turn on red follows the same rule as a right turn on red.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"Right on red is allowed at most intersections after a full stop, but left on red only from one one-way street onto another.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Right on red often; left on red rarely.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are on a two-way street at a steady red and want to turn left onto a one-way street. Is a left on red allowed?","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"No. Both streets must be one-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"rationale":{"text":"Left on red works only when turning from one one-way street onto another, after stopping and yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"The steady lights","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady red.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Turns on red.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Steady yellow and green.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the three steady signal lights and the turns they allow. Steady red seems simple, but it comes with two turning rules that are tested often: right on red and the much narrower left on red. Steady yellow is a warning, and how you respond depends on where you are when it appears. Steady green gives you permission to go, but not before yielding to anyone already in your path. As we go, notice how every light, even green, carries a duty to yield. That duty is what keeps a signal-controlled intersection safe for everyone.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Steady red","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop and wait for green.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Right on red after stopping and yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Unless a sign forbids it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"At a steady red light, stop and wait for green. There is one common exception: after stopping and yielding to pedestrians and traffic, a right turn on red is allowed unless a sign forbids it. Notice the order. You stop first, completely, then you yield, and only then do you turn. A rolling right turn on red is not allowed. And if a sign says no turn on red, the exception disappears and you wait for green like everyone else. Pedestrians in the crosswalk you are about to cross always go first, even when the turn itself is legal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Left on red","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Both streets one-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Stop and yield first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},{"text":"No sign against it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Turning left on red is far more limited. It is legal only when both streets are one-way, going from one onto the other, after you stop and yield, and only if no sign prohibits it. So from a two-way street, there is no left on red, even onto a one-way street. The reason is safety: on a one-way street turning left onto another one-way street, the left turn does not cross oncoming traffic, much like a right turn on a two-way street. When the streets are not both one-way, a left on red would cut across traffic coming toward you.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Right on red versus left","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right on red: most intersections.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Left on red: one-way onto one-way only.","fact_ids":["sec05-R03","sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Questions often describe a driver on a two-way street hoping to turn left on red onto a one-way street, and offer an answer saying it is allowed. It is not, because both streets must be one-way. Someone finishing a turn or a pedestrian still crossing must be allowed to finish before you move.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Left on red?","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two-way street, steady red.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Turning left onto a one-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Is it allowed?","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are stopped at a steady red light on a two-way street, and you want to turn left onto a one-way street. No. Left on red is legal only when both streets are one-way, turning from one onto the other, after you stop and yield, and only if no sign prohibits it. Here your street is two-way, so you must wait for green. A right turn on red, by contrast, would be allowed after a full stop and yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Steady lights recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red: stop; right on red after yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Left on red: one-way to one-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Yellow warns; green still yields.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R03","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review.
